mcqs.question: Why can't Broken Access Control be fixed by a single library or setting the way SameSite cookies mostly close CSRF?
options: Because access control bugs are always caused by outdated dependencies
Because it requires TLS to be configured correctly on every server
Because every endpoint touching user-specific or privileged data needs its own correct check, so there's no single point of enforcement to fix once
Because it can only be exploited through browser developer tools
mcqs.explanation: Unlike a cookie attribute that applies uniformly, authorization has to be verified per endpoint against that endpoint's specific resource, so one missing check on one route out of hundreds is enough to be exploitable. It isn't tied to dependency versions, TLS configuration, or browser dev tools specifically.

mcqs.question: Changing `/orders/1234` to `/orders/1235` in the URL reveals another user's order. What is the underlying bug?
options: The order IDs are not encrypted in the URL
The session cookie is being shared between different users' browsers
The database is missing an index on the orders table
The endpoint checks that the requester is logged in but never checks that the requested order belongs to that requester
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic IDOR pattern: authentication succeeds (the requester really is logged in) but authorization never runs — the query fetches by ID alone instead of by ID and owner together. Encryption of the URL, a missing index, and cookie sharing between users are unrelated to this failure.

mcqs.question: An admin export route works for any authenticated user who guesses its URL, even though the admin UI only shows the button to admins. What's the root cause?
options: The route relies on the UI not linking to it instead of verifying the caller's role at the server
The route is missing input validation on its parameters
The route uses an outdated authentication library
The route doesn't use HTTPS, allowing anyone to intercept the request
mcqs.explanation: The route was designed assuming access control lives in which links the UI renders, rather than enforcing a role check at the server boundary where the request actually lands — exactly the missing function-level authorization pattern. Input validation, authentication library version, and transport encryption aren't what's failing here.

mcqs.question: A regular user discovers they can reach an admin-only 'delete any account' endpoint. Is this horizontal or vertical privilege escalation?
options: Horizontal, because it involves an account, similar to the IDOR example
Neither, since privilege escalation only applies to database-level permissions
Vertical, because the user reaches functionality intended for a higher privilege level than their own
Horizontal, because it doesn't grant access to any specific user's private data
mcqs.explanation: Vertical escalation means reaching capability meant for a higher privilege tier — exactly what happens when a regular user reaches admin-only functionality, regardless of whether that functionality touches a specific account. It isn't horizontal (that would be reaching another same-tier user's own data), and privilege escalation isn't restricted to database-level permissions.

mcqs.question: A React app hides the 'Delete User' button unless `user.role === 'admin'`. Is this a sufficient access control?
options: Yes, since the button is never rendered for non-admins in the browser
No — but only because React specifically is known to be insecure for conditional rendering
Yes, as long as the check also runs on every page load
No — the client is under the attacker's control, so anyone can call the underlying API directly, bypassing the UI entirely
mcqs.explanation: Anything running in the browser, including a hidden button, is good UX but not security, since an attacker can call the underlying API directly with a tool like curl regardless of what the UI renders. Repeating the check on every page load doesn't change that it's still client-side, and this isn't a React-specific weakness — it applies to any client-side framework.

mcqs.question: A team ships an admin-only route without any server-side role check, reasoning that since no UI link points to it, nobody will find it. What kind of defense is this, and why does it fail?
options: It's rate limiting, and it fails because rate limits don't apply to admin routes
It's security through obscurity, and it fails because URLs leak via history, JavaScript bundles, and straightforward guessing, plus automated scanners crawl for exactly this
It's encryption, and it fails because the route isn't served over HTTPS
It's a valid access control as long as the URL is sufficiently long and random
mcqs.explanation: Hiding a route without a rendered link is obscurity, not enforcement, and it reliably fails because URLs surface through browser history, referrer headers, JavaScript source, and guessing from adjacent known routes — exactly what automated scanners look for. It isn't a rate-limiting or encryption issue, and length or randomness of the URL doesn't substitute for an actual authorization check.
